A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ExploraCoder and are readable throughout, including their appendices. Equations, experiments, figures, tables, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original code-generation results, component ablations, retrieval experiments, and execution case studies in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original code-generation results and ablations, plus new agentic comparisons, computational-cost measurements, sampling experiments, and MonkBeatEval results.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 refines the stated experience-selection rule: v1 randomly selects an executable candidate, whereas v2 prioritizes executable candidates with valid outputs. The planning, retrieval, chained exploration, optional debugging, and final-generation framework otherwise remains substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds MonkBeatEval, comprising 50 multi-API problems using transformed Pandas and NumPy APIs, extending evaluation beyond Torchdata. It removes the separate Torchdata-AR API-retrieval evaluation from v1 Appendix A.7. Torchdata-Manual's reported sample-count expansion concerns E3 rather than new task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Tables 2–3 add evaluated ReAct and KnowAgent baselines to both Torchdata comparisons, substantially broadening comparison with agentic approaches. The existing retrieval baselines remain; v1's Self-Repair already used CAPIR retrieval and is renamed CAPIR + Self-Repair, rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: The reported planning setting changes from kD=5 to 4. Section 4 and Table 9 report 100 Torchdata-Manual problems instead of 50, although Appendix A.4 still says 50. New protocols include agent reasoning budgets of 16/21 steps and a 50-problem sampling study extending CAPIR evaluation through k=130. The conflicting dataset descriptions prevent fully reconciling the evaluated sample count.

E4.justification: v2 adds computational-efficiency comparisons and an approximately token-matched sampling analysis testing whether cheaper CAPIR can catch up through additional candidates. It removes v1's retrieval-model, indexing, and single-versus-multiple-subtask retrieval analyses, plus the aggregate CoAE-success table. Component ablations, correlation plots, planning statistics, and detailed execution cases largely remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent experimental repeat counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's sampling study varies solution-candidate budgets; Figure 2's range lines describe differences between two models rather than uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: Shared main-table Torchdata-Github scores remain unchanged, but many Manual results are replaced under the revised reported dataset size: GPT-3.5 ExploraCoder pass@10 changes from 11.61% to 13.84%. Agentic, MonkBeatEval, cost, and sampling results are added; retrieval-recall results are removed. v2 Table 6 also appears to interchange CAPIR and EpiGen aggregate scores relative to Tables 2–3.

T1.justification: The framework's defining Equations 1–7 and mathematical task formulation remain substantively unchanged. Appendix A.1.2 adds a limited analytical cost model, including expected model-call expressions based on debugging probabilities, such as (1+5p1)n+1 and 2p2n+2.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a training-free exploration framework and a complex multi-API benchmark. The abstract and introduction revise the headline pass@10 advantages from 11.24% and 14.07% to up to 11.99% and 17.28%, and broaden the comparison wording from naive RAG to retrieval-based approaches.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit limitations concerning model capability, documentation quality, and wasted computation without early termination, alongside substantive efficiency and agent-behavior interpretations. It also drops v1's qualification that lexically renamed APIs retain functionality already exposed to models, while using such transformations to support broader generalizability.

D1.justification: v2 documents agent tools, an eight-step trajectory example, reasoning budgets, token-accounting procedures, and MonkBeatEval's bidirectional transformations. It newly describes documentation masking and states that code/data are available at a changed repository, replacing v1's future-release statement. Conversely, deleting v1 Appendix A.7 removes the named embedding model and retrieval-index construction recipe.

R1.justification: v2 substantially recasts positioning around preactive, reactive, and exploratory planning, replacing much of v1's SWE-Bench-agent and novelty discussion with a broader framework comparison. It adds substantive engagement with ReAct, KnowAgent, inference-time sampling, and other code-generation literature, while removing several previously discussed works.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten or condensed. The benchmark discussion is reordered, a dedicated limitations section is added, and the appendices are reorganized around comparisons, efficiency, quantitative analyses, and benchmark construction.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, merges v1 Tables 2–3 into Table 1, and replaces the detailed self-debug comparison table with a mean-and-range bar chart. It compresses the ablation table, relocates benchmark statistics, adds feature/cost/sampling/MonkBeatEval tables, and reformats the code listings.

improvement.justification: The added cross-library evaluation, agentic baselines, and approximately token-matched sampling study substantially strengthen validation, addressing v1's limited evidence about generalizability and computational fairness. Explicit limitations also improve assessment of applicability. These gains outweigh the loss of retrieval-analysis details, although the conflicting 50/100-problem descriptions and apparent CAPIR/EpiGen score interchange remain material reporting weaknesses.
